newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein's trip to Israel not political, analysts.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein's trip to Israel not political, analysts.

text.p: King Hussein's condolence visit to Jerusalem must not be seen as a political retreat from his bitter criticism last week of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Jordanian analysts said on Sunday.
They said the king's trip should be viewed as a humanitarian gesture after a Jordanian soldier gunned down seven Israeli teenagers, not a thawing of political ties.
"I think one should distinguish between the humanitarian attitude, which is desirable, and the political facts," said one political analyst, who declined to be named.

The king's visit came a day before Israeli bulldozers were due to start building Jewish settlements around Arab East Jerusalem and exactly a week after he accused Netanyahu of pushing the Middle East "towards an abyss of bloodshed".
State television showed the king kneeling next to relatives of one of the Israeli victims, holding their hands as Netanyahu looked on at his side.

"He is taking a risk by going because we don't know what the reaction will be in Jordan or in Israel -- whether it might be considered a sign of weakness," said Hani Hourani, head of the Amman-based New Jordan Centre.
"But he is not changing his mind about his criticism of Netanyahu," he said.
Officials in Jordan were swift to condemn the killing of the seven Israelis three days ago and most Jordanians said they rejected any attack on young children.
But criticism of the shooting has been tinged by a perception that the world is always quicker to sympathise with Israeli rather than Arab victims.

"What about the 100 people killed in Qana?" was the curt reply from a member of Jordan's Islamic Action Front when asked for reaction to Thursday's shooting. Around 100 Lebanese civilians were killed by Israeli shelling at a United Nations camp in the southern Lebanese village of Qana in 1996.
"I hope the king will not over-react in his sympathy, the Jordanians will not like it," a liberal academic said.
"The attack should not have been against young innocent children but against Netanyahu who is stubborn and a tyrant," an elderly farmer said near the scene of Thursday's attack.

Ibrahim Izzedine, a former government minister, said Israel's insistence on going ahead with building a Jerusalem settlement was souring a two-year peace treaty with Jordan already eroded in Jordanian eyes by a lack of material returns.
"The problem is being crystallised in Jerusalem," Izzedine told Reuters, adding that the 1994 treaty now looked more like a non-aggression pact than a peace accord between good neighbours.
"It's now just an end of belligerency, rather than a treaty opening up relations between the countries," he said. "This is the thinking in the political psyche and the population as a whole."

The king's visit to Jerusalem was his second to Israel in two months, after his last-minute shuttle from Gaza to Tel Aviv helped rescue a deal with Palestinians on further Israeli withdrawals from the West Bank.
But the brief spirit of compromise disappeared a few weeks later when Israel announced its next pullout from the West Bank would be much less than Palestinians had expected.

"They should not take peace with Jordan for granted," said Hourani, adding he considered himself a campaigner for peace. "We cannot make it a warm peace if they are not going to settle with the Palestinians."
